docs.title: Jose Bernardo Martinez Morales
docs.text:
Robotics Software Engineer · Granada, Spain

Robotics software engineer with a strong focus on ROS 2, real-time control, and system integration for robotic platforms. I have experience building and maintaining robust robotic software stacks, from simulation and testing to deployment on real hardware.

My work spans C++ and Python development, ROS/ROS 2 middleware, and control for manipulators and mobile robots. I’m particularly interested in reliable autonomy, sim-to-real transfer, and scalable robotic architectures. Currently exploring reinforcement learning and its applications in robotics

docs.title: Cerebellar SNN: motor learning from simulation to real robots
docs.text:
A cerebellum model of 70,000+ neurons that learns torque control and moves to real robots by switching one ROS topic.

Franka Research 3 driven by the SNN on a Jetson Xavier, circular trajectory Baxter, the hardest case (elastic joints) 1 · Learning starts in simulation: erratic, potentially damaging motions 2 · Once stable, weights are saved (~450 trials, ~30 min) 3 · Weights loaded on the real robot by changing only the ROS topic 4 · After ~80 more trials, the error converges
  • Requirement: learn joint torque control in real time, on robots with different dynamics, without damaging them.
  • Key decisions: NRP/ROS bridge so sim-to-real is a topic change; learn in simulation first; bounded torque output by design; network size and rate scaled per platform; Vicon as independent ground truth.
  • My work: Gazebo–EDLUT bridge, GPU and Jetson Xavier/Orin deployment, real-robot tests on Franka Research 3, Baxter and Sawyer.
  • Result: ~450 trials (~30 min) in simulation, then ~80 trials on the real robot until the error converged.
  • Control rate: PC 500 Hz · Jetson Orin 250 Hz · Jetson Xavier 100 Hz.

docs.title: Formation control with obstacle avoidance
docs.text:
Robots keep a formation and avoid obstacles, with continuous velocities at all times.

Core idea: obstacle avoidance (high priority) over formation tracking (low priority), with a smooth transition
  • Core idea: two prioritized tasks. Obstacle avoidance (high priority, active only near obstacles) over formation tracking (low priority, consensus). A smooth transition keeps velocities continuous.
  • Distributed: neighbor data and local obstacle sensing only. No global frame, no map. Stability proven.
  • Real robots: Pioneer 3DX leader + 2 TurtleBot 2, triangular formation, ROS over WiFi, OptiTrack.
  • Linear trajectory (30 s): a follower evades a fixed obstacle at ~18 s; the group recovers the formation.
  • Circular trajectory (R 1.1 m, 70 s): evasion at ~53–65 s; tracking errors converge to zero.
  • My role: first author; software, methodology, validation. Later migrated the full stack to ROS 2 and Gazebo Sim (Harmonic).

▶ Video: linear trajectory ▶ Video: circular trajectory 📄 Paper (Sensors 2021)

Project 1 · Neurorobotics

docs.title: Cerebellar SNN: motor learning from simulation to real robots
docs.text:
A 70,000+ neuron spiking cerebellum model that learns joint torque control in simulation and finishes learning on three real robots, at up to 500 Hz.

ROSEDLUTGazeboNeurorobotics PlatformGPUJetson Xavier / OrinVicon Model Spiking neural network (SNN) mirroring the cerebellar circuit, 70,000+ neurons, joint torque output Robots Franka Research 3, Baxter, Sawyer Compute Desktop PC with GPU, Jetson Orin, Jetson Xavier Control rate PC 500 Hz · Jetson Orin 250 Hz · Jetson Xavier 100 Hz Sim-to-real ~450 trials (~30 min) in simulation, then ~80 trials on the real robot until the error converged My role Simulator bridge, GPU and Jetson deployment, real-robot experiments Franka Research 3 driven by the SNN on a Jetson Xavier, circular trajectory Baxter, the hardest of the three robots

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Learn joint torque control online with a cerebellum-inspired SNN.
  • Run in real time: up to 500 Hz on a desktop GPU, and on embedded Jetson boards.
  • Never damage the robot while the network is still learning.
  • One controller for several robots with different, partly elastic dynamics.
  • Measure performance independently of the robot's own sensors.

docs.title: The model
docs.text:
The network mirrors the cerebellar circuit (mossy fibers, granule cells, Purkinje cells, climbing fibers and deep cerebellar nuclei). It receives sensory input and an error (teaching) signal, and improves a movement by repeating it: supervised, trial-by-trial learning. Its output is a joint torque command, which is what makes this a real-time, safety-critical systems problem.

Cerebellar microcircuit: parallel fibers, granule, Purkinje and nuclear cells The simplified model: sensory input, teaching signal, motor output

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
Network hostDesktop PC or Jetson Xavier / Orinruns the SNN (EDLUT, GPU) ⟶torques over ROS Robot or GazeboFranka Research 3 · Baxter · Sawyer ⟶end-effector pose Vicon camerasindependent ground truth

The SNN runs in EDLUT and the robot in Gazebo or on hardware; the Neurorobotics Platform (NRP) connects them over ROS. A separate PC handles live plots so it does not load the network host.

Simulated arm learning a trajectory: error plots (top) and layer activity (bottom)

docs.title: Key design decisions
docs.text: Decision Alternative Rationale Couple EDLUT and Gazebo through the NRP over ROS A custom simulator coupling One ROS interface for simulation and hardware, so moving to the real robot is a topic change, not a code change Learn in simulation first, then continue on hardware Learn directly on the robot Early learning produces erratic torques; simulation absorbs them, and only a stable network reaches the motors Safety by design: the network's torque output is bounded An external safety filter added afterwards The controller cannot command torques outside its range, even while learning Scale network size and update rate per platform One configuration everywhere Keeps real time on each target: PC 500 Hz, Orin 250 Hz, Xavier 100 Hz Learn at joint level, validate in Cartesian space with Vicon Rely on the robot's own encoders An independent measurement of what the end effector actually does Test on three cobots (Franka, Baxter, Sawyer) Tune for a single robot Shows the controller generalizes, including Baxter's elastic joints Sawyer Franka Research 3 Baxter NVIDIA Jetson Xavier / Orin

docs.title: Sim-to-real transfer
docs.text:
1 · Learning starts in simulation, where erratic motions are harmless 2 · Once learning is stable, the weights are saved 3 · The same network is loaded on the real robot by changing only the ROS topic 4 · After ~80 more trials the error converges
  1. Simulation: ~450 trials of a 4 s trajectory, about 30 minutes, until learning is stable.
  2. Save the weights and load them on the real robot, changing only the ROS topic.
  3. Real robot: learning continues, and the error converges after ~80 more trials.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Franka Research 3 tracking a circular trajectory with the network running on a Jetson Xavier, verified with Vicon.
  • Baxter, the most demanding dynamics of the three because of its external springs, controlled by the same network.
  • Real-time control at 500 Hz (PC), 250 Hz (Jetson Orin) and 100 Hz (Jetson Xavier).

docs.title: Dual-actuation arm: remote high-level interface
docs.text:
A remote ROS 2 interface that lets off-board neural controllers drive a research arm with muscle-like actuators, while the on-board controller stays pure C++.

RustZenohROS 2C++Raspberry Pi 4Torque control Robot Research prototype with two actuators per joint (agonist and antagonist), designed from scratch What I built The remote side: a ROS 2 high-level interface on the PC and the command link to the arm Stack ROS 2 on the remote PC, Zenoh transport (Rust), pure C++ on the Raspberry Pi 4 Targets 1 kHz loop, torque control Context EPFL BioRobotics Laboratory visit (2025), with KM-RoBoTa on the hardware deployment

docs.title: The robot
docs.text:
Each joint has an agonist and an antagonist actuator, mimicking human muscles. A pair of opposing actuators makes adjustable joint stiffness possible. The robot was designed from scratch; I joined when the software layer had to be built.

Alpha version New version (CAD)

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Run neural controllers off-board: the Raspberry Pi 4 has no GPU.
  • Expose the arm to ROS 2 users on a remote PC.
  • Keep the on-board software pure C++, with no ROS 2 dependency.
  • Exchange commands, forward and inverse kinematics between both computers.
  • Designed for a 1 kHz loop with torque control.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
Remote PCROS 2 interface + neural controllers ⇄Zenoh Raspberry Pi 4low-level control, pure C++ ⇄ Dual-actuation armagonist / antagonist actuators

Controllers on the remote PC use a standard ROS 2 interface. Zenoh carries commands and state between the PC and the Raspberry Pi, where the low-level controller runs in plain C++.

docs.title: Key design decisions
docs.text: Decision Alternative Rationale No ROS 2 on the Raspberry Pi: on-board software in pure C++ (team decision) Run ROS 2 on the robot Keeps the embedded side lean and independent of the ROS 2 stack Zenoh as the communication layer between PC and robot ROS 2 / DDS end to end Lets ROS 2 users on the PC reach a robot that does not run ROS 2, keeping both sides as compatible as possible Neural controllers on the remote PC Run them on board The Raspberry Pi has no GPU; the PC provides the compute ROS 2 interface on the remote side A custom API Any ROS 2 controller or tool can drive the arm without knowing the transport

docs.title: Formation control with obstacle avoidance
docs.text:
Robots keep a formation while following a leader and avoid obstacles, with continuous velocities at all times. Tested on three real robots.

ROSROS 2Gazebo Sim (Harmonic)Consensus controlOptiTrackTurtleBot 2Pioneer 3DX Paper J. B. Martinez, H. M. Becerra and D. Gomez-Gutierrez. Formation tracking control and obstacle avoidance of unicycle-type robots guaranteeing continuous velocities. Sensors 2021, 21(13), 4374 My role First author. Software, methodology, validation Robots Pioneer 3DX (leader) + 2 TurtleBot 2 (followers), differential-drive Software ROS over WiFi, positions from an OptiTrack motion-capture system Later Full stack migrated to ROS 2 and Gazebo Sim (Harmonic), refactoring node architecture and communication patterns

📄 Read the paper ▶ Video: linear trajectory ▶ Video: circular trajectory

docs.title: The core idea: two prioritized tasks
docs.text:
A group of mobile robots must keep a formation while a leader follows a trajectory, and avoid obstacles, including each other. The scheme solves both tasks simultaneously with a hierarchy:

Obstacle avoidancehigh priority, active only near an obstacle Formation trackinglow priority, consensus with the leader included ⟶ Hierarchical task controlsmooth transition function h(t) ⟶ Continuous velocitiesfor every robot
  • Obstacle avoidance has the higher priority and only activates when a robot gets close to an obstacle, inside a security distance.
  • Formation tracking has the lower priority and always runs. It is based on consensus, with the leader included as part of the formation.
  • A smooth transition function between the two keeps every robot's velocity continuous, even when avoidance switches on or off, and stability is proven during the transition.
  • It is fully distributed: each robot needs only relative information from its neighbors and local obstacle measurements, so no global coordinate system or map is required.
  • It is scalable to many robots and generic: any desired formation can be defined.

docs.title: Key design decisions
docs.text:
Decision Alternative Rationale Hierarchical task control: avoidance over formation tracking A single controller that blends both objectives Avoidance always takes precedence near an obstacle, and the smooth transition keeps velocities continuous with proven stability Consensus-based formation tracking Centralized control in a global frame Fully distributed: each robot uses only relative neighbor data and local sensing, with no global frame or map

The paper also evaluates the scheme in simulation with 4 and 10 agents and in environments with unknown polygonal obstacles, before the real-robot experiments below.

docs.title: Real-robot experiments
docs.text:
Setup. A Pioneer 3DX is the leader and two TurtleBot 2 are the followers, in a triangular formation at 0.7 m displacement from the leader. Each robot is connected via WiFi to a computer where the velocity commands are computed in a distributed way using ROS: each agent publishes its computed velocities and reads those of its neighbors. Robot and obstacle positions come from an OptiTrack system. The gains were γ = 0.8 (tracking), λ = 0.8 (evasion) and k = 0.12 (consensus).

Linear trajectory (30 s)

  • The leader tracks a straight line with a fixed obstacle nearby (security distance 0.4 m).
  • One follower evades the obstacle at about 18 s, which also moves the others, with only a small effect on the leader.
  • The group recovers the formation and the virtual agents reach consensus at the final point.
  • Computed velocities stay continuous throughout, thanks to the transition function.

▶ Watch the video

Circular trajectory (radius 1.1 m, 70 s)

  • The leader tracks a circle that returns to its starting point, with a fixed obstacle (security distance 0.55 m).
  • The robots deviate around the obstacle between about 53 s and 65 s, and then return to the formation.
  • After the avoidance finishes, tracking and consensus errors converge to zero, as proven in the paper.
  • Velocities again stay continuous throughout.

▶ Watch the video

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Existing schemes rarely combine all of the following: fully distributed, scalable, generic in the formation, no need for a global frame or a map, and continuous velocities when obstacle avoidance activates. The hierarchical formulation covers all of them at once, and it is the first time, to the authors' knowledge, that distributed formation tracking is combined with obstacle avoidance in this way.

Project 3 · Mobile manipulation

docs.title: TIAGo Pro: a ROS 2 torque interface for both arms
docs.text:
Safe torque control of both TIAGo Pro arms over ROS 2 at 500 Hz, validated on the real robot.

ROS 2ros2_controlMoveIt 2State machineGazebo ClassicDockerC++Python Outcome External controllers (e.g. neural controllers) can command joint torques on both arms through ROS 2 topics What I built A ROS 2 mode-manager node on top of ros2_control: one active controller per arm (position, velocity or effort), selected by a state machine Control rate 500 Hz effort control, tested on the real robot Safety Position hold at startup, 0.5 s command watchdog that falls back to position hold Stack C++ and Python nodes, ros2_control, MoveIt 2, Gazebo Classic, Docker Torque control running on the real TIAGo Pro

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Stream joint torques from an external controller over ROS 2 topics at 500 Hz.
  • Exactly one controller owns each arm at any time; the two arms are independent.
  • Fail safe: if the command stream stops, the arm holds its position.
  • Leave the vendor software stack unmodified.
  • A reproducible development and deployment environment.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
User controllerpublishes torques or joint commands ⟶ROS 2 topics Mode managerstate machine, one mode per arm ⟶controller_manager Arm controllersposition · velocity · effort ⟶ TIAGo Pro armsor Gazebo simulation

Users publish commands on per-arm topics (for example arm_left_effort_joint_controller/commands) and request a mode through the interface. The mode manager runs one state machine per arm and asks controller_manager to activate the matching ros2_control controller. All three controllers can be loaded and waiting, but only the active one claims the arm's joint interfaces.

docs.title: Key design decisions
docs.text: Decision Alternative Rationale Reuse ros2_control controllers through controller_manager Write a custom hardware interface Keeps the vendor's tested hardware layer untouched; the work stays in user space Per-arm state machine decides which controller is active Users start and stop controllers by hand Several controllers can be loaded and waiting, but only one can claim an arm's joint interfaces. The state machine makes ownership explicit and every switch goes through the same safety logic Topic streaming for commands Services or actions Continuous 500 Hz command stream; any external controller can publish without depending on my code Position hold as the startup and fallback state Start in effort mode The arm is supported before the first torque command arrives 0.5 s command watchdog back to position hold No timeout, or a very short one Tolerates transport delays without false triggers, but is short enough to stop the arm before it can fall or self-collide. Tuned empirically on the robot arm_{side} parameterized nodes (declare_parameter) One copy of the code per arm A single binary controls either arm, selected at launch without recompiling Docker environment Native install on the robot PC Reproducible setup; the robot's own dependencies, shared by all its controllers, stay untouched

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
• Developed and tested first in Gazebo, then deployed on the real robot.
  • Effort control running at 500 Hz on the real robot (video above). The arms are independent: one can run in torque mode while the other holds position.

docs.title: Supporting work
docs.text:
• ROS 1 → ROS 2 / MoveIt 2 migration. The TIAGo Pro has no ROS 1 support, and the controllers needed test trajectories, so I ported the trajectory-planning code to MoveIt 2 (with a background rclpy executor thread, as MoveIt 2 requires).
  • Trajectory dispatcher. Four scripts (circle, infinity, square, target reaching) unified into dual_arm_trajectory.py, selected with trajectory:=circle, solving inverse kinematics for both arms.
  • Full-body controllers. full_controllers:=true also brings up head, torso and mobile base, which prevents drift from the arms' reaction forces; the joint-state broadcaster discovers every joint from the URDF.

Project 4 · Medical robotics

docs.title: Tumor localization by bioimpedance palpation
docs.text:
A surgical robot locates a tumor by palpation and recovers its shape with only 25–50% of the samples, at recall above 90%.

dVRK PSM2ROSRVizMATLABGaussian ProcessElectrical bioimpedanceRealSense Goal Locate a tumor beneath the tissue surface, where vision cannot see, for minimally invasive surgery Robot da Vinci Research Kit (dVRK), patient-side manipulator PSM2 Sensing Electrical bioimpedance (EBI) probe in direct tissue contact Planner Gaussian Process active area search (MATLAB) Result Tumor shape reconstructed with 25–50% of the samples, recall >90% against ground truth Context Visiting researcher, Altair Robotics Laboratory, Verona (Jan – Jul 2020) Experimental setup: dVRK PSM2 palpating a sponge phantom with fiducial markers

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Find and outline a tumor by touch, using bioimpedance (abnormal tissue reads differently from healthy tissue).
  • Minimize the number of palpations compared with an exhaustive sweep.
  • Validate the software before any trial on the physical robot.
  • Measure accuracy against an exhaustive ground truth and show the result in 3D.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
1 · 3D acquisitionROI point cloud and optical markers ⟶ 2 · Kinematics & simulationdVRK PSM2 control in RViz / ROS ⟶ 3 · Robotic palpationEBI probe in direct tissue contact ⟶ 4 · Active plannerGaussian Process (MATLAB) ⟶ 5 · Map & validationground truth vs estimate

ROS nodes synchronize the sensor, the manipulator and the planner. The region of interest is discretized in a 20 × 20 grid (400 points); the planner decides which cells actually need palpation.

docs.title: Key design decisions
docs.text: Decision Alternative Rationale Gaussian Process active area search picks the next point to palpate Exhaustive 20 × 20 sweep Reconstructs the tumor with 25–50% of the samples at recall above 90%, so far fewer contacts with the tissue ROS-based EBI sensor emulator and an RViz model of the arm Develop directly on the hardware The whole pipeline (kinematics, safe trajectories, workspace, planner) is validated before any physical trial Fiducial markers + RealSense point cloud 2D maps only Calibrates the camera and overlays the estimate on the 3D surface for validation Digital model of the da Vinci arm in RViz 400-point grid with the simulated tumor (green cylinder)

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Ground truth stiffness map vs active area search, with the RViz and MATLAB views 3D surface map: depth sensor, 4 fiducial markers, circular region of interest Ground truth: exhaustive impedance map over the 3D relief Planned estimate: reduced samples, same position and shape
  • The estimate reproduces the position and concentric shape of the tumor core (the high-impedance red-yellow region), with recall above 90% against the exhaustive ground truth.
  • Achieved with 25–50% of the samples of a full sweep.
  • Reported experiments use a sponge phantom, with liquid soap and water to create the impedance contrast.
